added_sections.title: A kitchen figure and a courtyard arrangement
added_sections.text: Sarangi describes a dried-fish figure dressed as a bride, seated on a stool in a kitchen corner beside kanji and dried-fish rai. Mahakud describes evening worship near the tulasi platform, a small water-filled pit and seven dressed fish figures. These are author-specific descriptions with no identified fieldwork locality. Their different settings should remain visible rather than be combined into one ritual sequence.
added_sections.locator: Sarangi Kanji Anla passage / web172; Mahakud ritual-procedure paragraph / web88

added_sections.title: After the offering: children and separate ritual materials
added_sections.text: Mahakud lists rice, dal, kanji, a taro–radish–dried-fish curry and two chakuli pithas. He describes feeding the offerings to the children for whom the vow was made, then burying or immersing the remainder. Poi stalks placed beside the fish figures have a separate non-sharing rule in his account. This is an attributed description, not a disposal instruction or a claim about every household.

added_sections.title: Care expressed through a meal
added_sections.text: Read alongside the mother’s appeal in the story, feeding the intended children gives the offering a concrete relationship: the household’s hope is expressed through preparing and sharing food. This is an editorial interpretation of the published retelling. It does not establish an observed benefit, a universal meaning or permission to enter private worship.

added_sections.title: Names that should stay distinct
added_sections.text: Kanji Anla remains a separate observance from Alana and Anla Navami. Sarangi discusses Anla Navami in a Kartika passage and Kanji Anla after Prathamastami in Margasira. Similar spelling and a shared food vocabulary do not prove that these are interchangeable names.
added_sections.locator: Kartika Anla Navami passage / web161; Prathamastami–Kanji Anla passage / web172
